Posted March 12, 2001
Excerpts from " Bush neglects drug war. " By Don Feder

" Almost seven weeks into his administration, President George Bush has yet to appoint a drug czar. For a nation in which addiction has become a chronic problem and drugs take a devastating toll, that does not inspire confidence… "

(MarijuanaNews note: This column appeared on WorldNetDaily.com

However, this story is not about venom overdoses. If it were, Feder would have his own page at the Poison Control Center. Consequently, I have omitted most of his political fantasies.

The point here is that Feder simply does not know what he is talking about and is quite happy to give false evidence against the people he hates.)

" Drug-related emergency-room admissions are at a historic high -- over 555,000 in 1999. "

(MarijuanaNews note: Actually, these are " episodes " not admissions, and the number has been around 500,000 for the last several years. The most common cases – roughly one third -- were " alcohol used in combination with another drug. " Alcohol alone accounted for far more than all of these " drug-related episodes " combined.

Of course, 37 percent were attempted suicides, which really is another problem.

However, to put this in context, consider that basketball accounted for 644,921 emergency room visits in 1997!)

(MarijuanaNews note: There is not the slightest basis in fact for this statement. Oddly, Barry McCaffrey, the former Drug Czar, claimed only that " Each year drug use exacts $110 billion in social costs. "

In reality, the study McCaffrey used to estimate a $110 billion social cost states that sixty percent (60%) of those costs are due to drug-related law enforcement, incarceration and crime. These are the costs created by prohibition.

Only 3% of drug costs were from victims of drug-related crime, and less than 40% of the $110 billion social costs actually are due to the health impact of drugs and much of that is also caused by prohibition.

Unless Feder has access to data that McCaffrey did not have, or McCaffrey was understating the cost of " drug abuse " – both very unlikely – then Feder’s numbers are even more absurd than the Czar’s.)

(MarijuanaNews note: Yeah, sure. There is more spent every day on prohibitionist propaganda than the annual budgets of the all the reform groups combined.)

" Wanted: a drug czar like William J. Bennett -- who will bang the bully pulpit till the wood splits, confront the drug lobby in the ballot arena, and not neglect supply reduction and punishment…

As Bennett pointed out in a Feb. 18 Washington Post piece, treatment (which drug defeatists would substitute for everything else) has a modest success rate.

Only half who begin treatment programs complete them, and 25 percent of those relapse within five years. Thus, just 38 percent who enter rehab are cured. Besides, many addicts would never get treatment without a prison sentence hanging over their heads. Limiting supply, through interdiction and the incarceration of dealers, is far more effective. "

However, treatment seemed to work for Bennett. When he was Drug Czar he was on nicotine maintenance, even as he was denouncing " drug addicts. " )

" The key to success is a coordinated approach -- reduce supplies, limit sources and make punishment so severe that it deters casual users, from whose ranks hard-core addicts come. "

(MarijuanaNews note: When I first started smoking marijuana in Texas in 1967, the penalty was up to life in prison for possession of any amount. That was the period of the most rapid growth in marijuana use. But just what punishment would satisfy him? Let him spell this out. Tell us just what you want to do, Mr. Feder. How severe? Of course, one problem with harsh punishments is that the prohibitionists deny that anyone is being punished. This leads to what I call " stealth terrorism. " Punishment is no deterrence if no one even knows that people are being arrested.)

The leading cause of death for the age group between 15 and 25 was auto accidents at 9,828.

In 1998 the second leading cause of death for the age group between 15 and 25 was being shot with a guns not needles. That number was 4,559.

" Drugs " were not in the top ten.

According to the Centers for Disease Control, there were 19,515 non-traffic, alcohol-related fatalities in 1998. Tobacco-related diseases kill some 430,000 Americans annually.
Opiates killed 3,141.

Over-the-counter pain relievers kill thousands ever year, including children.

From The Journal of Pediatrics January, 1998;132:

At least 24 children in the United States have died and three have required liver transplants after receiving accidental overdoses of acetaminophen -- the most widely used medication for relief of pain and fever in children and infants. Researchers say parents should be advised about the dangers of exceeding the recommended doses of the drug, which are based on children's body weight. The report is a compilation of 55 documented cases of accidental liver toxicity in children attributed to acetaminophen given in doses above those recommended. Of the two dozen deaths, six were due to multiple acetaminophen doses slightly above weight-based recommendations. "

This probably only represents a fraction of the total number of cases, because hospitals are not required to report these deaths.

Of course, marijuana killed none directly. How many people died because they were denied medical access to marijuana is unknowable.)
